claim: For the sixth dimensionality reduction approach, a principal coordinates analysis of the distance matrix of the Jensen-Shannon divergence of OTU abundances was performed, selecting the first five coordinates.
source: For the sixth approach, we performed a principal coordinates analysis of the distance matrix of the Jensen-Shannon divergence (Endres and Schindelin, 2003) of OTU abundances using the 'dudi.pcoa' function from the ade4 package (Chessel et al., 2004; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), selecting the first five coordinates by inspecting the scree plot.
evidence: This describes another dimensionality reduction approach, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: For the seventh dimensionality reduction approach, a network representing significant correlations between OTU abundances was calculated with SparCC, and the network was partitioned into functional groups using functionInk.
source: For the seventh and final approach, we calculated a network representing significant correlations between OTU abundances inferred with SparCC (Friedman and Alm, 2012), considering only significant links (pseudo p-value<0.01, absolute value of the correlation coefficient > 0.2) leading to a network whose links represent either segregations (negative correlations) or aggregations (positive correlations) between species. Note that these links do not necessarily reflect ecological interactions, since correlations may be caused by bacteria's environmental preferences (Pascual-García et al., 2014). We next partitioned the network into functional groups using functionInk (Pascual-García and Bell, 2020b).
evidence: This describes the functional group approach to dimensionality reduction.

claim: functionInk is a community-detection method that classifies the nodes in the network clustering together those nodes sharing approximately the same number and type of links with respect to the same neighbours.
source: Briefly, functionInk is a community-detection method that classifies the nodes in the network clustering together those nodes sharing approximately the same number and type of links (aggregations and segregations in our case) with respect to the same neighbours.
evidence: This is a description of the functionInk method.

claim: Previous work observed that a classification of the samples according to their beta-diversity distance led to the identification of six community-classes, and that these classes had distinct functional and metagenomic signatures.
source: In previous work, we observed that a classification of the samples according to their beta-diversity distance, led to the identification of six community-classes, and that these classes had distinct functional and metagenomic signatures (Pascual-García and Bell, 2020a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: functionInk was run on the network finding an optimal partition at the maximum of the total partition density with 63 functional groups.
source: To identify these functional groups (Supplementary file 1), we run functionInk on the network finding an optimal partition at the maximum of the total partition density (Pascual-García and Bell, 2020b) with 63 functional groups.
evidence: This describes the application of functionInk to the data.

claim: For the final analysis, groups that had three or more members were selected, plus a group of functional groups of Paenibacillus species that had less than three members.
source: For the final analysis, we selected groups that had three or more members, plus a group of functional groups of Paenibacillus species that had less than three members.
evidence: This describes the selection criteria for functional groups.

claim: The selection process resulted in 19 functional groups (+ 1 variable representing the total mean abundance of remaining OTUs) as the representation of composition.
source: This whole process resulted in the selection of 19 functional groups (+ 1 variable representing the total mean abundance of remaining OTUs) as the representation of composition for this approach.
evidence: This describes the final output of the dimensionality reduction.

claim: The functional groups approach offered the best compromise in terms of variance explained vs. number of variables permuted.
source: This revealed functional groups approach (Pascual-García and Bell, 2020b) to be the most appropriate dimensionality reduction of composition to explain invasion, offering the best compromise in terms of variance explained vs. number of variables permuted.
evidence: This is a result from the comparison of dimensionality reduction approaches.

claim: Random forest regressions were used to find the most important individual explanatory variables for invader survival among many.
source: We used random forest regressions implemented using the 'randomForest' package (Liaw and Wiener, 2002) to find the most important individual explanatory variables for invader survival among many.
evidence: This describes the statistical method used.

claim: The main advantage of the random forest approach is that it is able to deal well with overfitting associated with having many explanatory variables.
source: The main advantage of the random forest approach for this was that it is able to deal well with overfitting associated with having many explanatory variables, by randomly shuffling the explanatory variables (and samples) permuted in each constituent regression tree and calculating their mean importance across the 'forest'.
evidence: This is a justification for the choice of statistical method.

claim: Random forests make few assumptions about the relationships between dependent and independent variables, accounting somewhat for non-independence and non-linearity.
source: It also makes few assumptions about the relationships between dependent and independent variables than parametric approaches, accounting somewhat for non-independence and non-linearity, for example.
evidence: This is a justification for the choice of statistical method.

claim: Structural equation models were used to test three scenarios to estimate the extent by which productivity mediated the effect of composition on invasion.
source: In our second part of our main analysis therefore, we sought to estimate the putative chain of causation between composition, productivity and invasion resistance using structural equation modelling (SEMs). This approach allowed us to test three scenarios to estimate the extent by which the productivity mediated the effect of composition on invasion (see main text).
evidence: This describes the use of structural equation modeling.

claim: A latent variable called 'Productivity' was created including cell yield at 7 and 14 days.
source: For these models, we created a latent variable called 'Productivity' including cell yield at 7 and 14 days.
evidence: This describes the construction of latent variables for the SEM.

claim: A latent variable called 'Composition' was created, including the abundance of the 19 (+1) functional groups and the Simpson's diversity of the OTUs.
source: We created another latent variable called 'Composition', including the abundance of the 19 (+1) functional groups and the Simpson's diversity of the OTUs.
evidence: This describes the construction of latent variables for the SEM.

claim: An 'Invasion' latent variable was created encapsulating all measurements of invader survival for both invaders at the three sampling points.
source: Finally, we created an 'Invasion' latent variable encapsulating all measurements of invader survival for both invaders at the three sampling points (24 hr, 96 hr, and 7 days after invasion).
evidence: This describes the construction of latent variables for the SEM.

claim: Sensitivity analyses were conducted as part of the SEM analysis to validate that the results on the raw data were not an artefact of random noise below the detection threshold of the luminescence assay.
source: We conducted sensitivity analyses as part of the SEM analysis, in order to validate that the results of the main analysis on the raw data were not an artefact of random noise below the detection threshold of the luminescence assay (which was converted into CFU/ml units).
evidence: This describes the sensitivity analysis approach.

claim: For the sensitivity analysis, under detection limit invader survival values were randomly shuffled 999 times by sampling the CFU-converted under detection limit data without replacement.
source: For this analysis, we randomly shuffled the under detection limit invader survival values 999 times by sampling the CFU-converted under detection limit data without replacement using the 'sample' function (base package).
evidence: This describes the sensitivity analysis method.

claim: When values below the detection limit were randomly shuffled, the model comparison very marginally supported the Complete over the Partial mediation model.
source: When values below the detection limit were randomly shuffled, the model comparison very marginally supported the Complete (mean ΔAIC = 0.97) over the Partial mediation model (mean ΔAIC = 0.02).
evidence: This is a result from the sensitivity analysis.

claim: The AIC values of all three models increased by 1383.71–1400 when values below the detection limit were randomly shuffled, indicating that at least some the values below the conservative detection limit were informative in the original models.
source: However, the AIC values of all three models also increased by 1383.71–1400 (i.e. fit decreased) - indicating that at least some the values below the conservative detection limit were informative in the original models.
evidence: This is a result from the sensitivity analysis.
